newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Erbakan avoids censure over Libya trip.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Erbakan avoids censure over Libya trip.

text.p: Turkey's parliament on Wednesday rejected a bid by the secularist opposition to force a confidence vote in Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan over his Islamist foreign policy.
Deputies voted by 275 to 256 not to hold a confidence vote over Erbakan's controversial trip 10 days ago to Libya -- the target of Western anger for alleged support of terrorism.
"Our government has become more powerful," Erbakan told reporters after the vote. "The government is in harmony and will serve the nation until the year 2000," he said.

The vote followed almost six hours of often tense debate in which the opposition hammered Erbakan, Turkey's first Islamist premier, for taking Ankara away from the West and toward the Moslem and Arab world.
The Libya trip also angered NATO-ally the United States.
"The junior coalition partner is fond of the West, the other partner (Erbakan) cannot take his heart and eyes off the dictatorial regimes of the East," leftist MP Ismail Cem told parliament.
Recent visits by Erbakan to Iran and Nigeria have also been slammed at home.

MPs accused him of bringing Turkey into disrepute during the Libya trip, where Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi gave him a dressing down in front of the television cameras about Turkey's treatment of its minority Kurds.
Deniz Baykal, a former foreign minister, said Erbakan had abandoned domestic responsibilities for adventures abroad.
"The new government rushed to a state which has a proven, close relation to terrorism...this was a mistake," he said.
His remarks touched off tit-for-tat charges between government and opposition MPs, delaying a vote on the censure motion to allow the right to reply.
Erbakan did not take the podium. A close aide defended the "eastern" foreign policy
"If you look around you will see that developed countries are the ones at peace with their neighbours," State Minister Abdullah Gul said in the debate.
"We are in close contact with Iran, Iraq and Syria...to set up a security ring," he said.
The Turkish military and secularist establishment often accuses Tehran and Damascus of backing Kurdish rebels fighting for self-rule in southeast Turkey.
Despite the public pasting, Erbakan's pro-Western coalition partner Tansu Ciller remained confident ahead of the vote.
"As long as the coalition protocol exists the government will continue," Ciller told MPs from her True Path Party (DYP) before the debate.
The result was never seriously in doubt. Erbakan's Welfare Party, whose iron discipline effectively bars dissent, boasts 160 MPs.
Ciller had ordered her 120 deputies to back the government, giving it a margin of four seats beyond the 276 needed to guarantee victory.
